summary: Describes how an IKEv2 server and a Diameter server can interact using shared keys. IKEv2 sets up IPsec security associations and supports several authentication methods, and this document covers the case where a shared key is used. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Two guards share a secret password so one can check visitors for the other. This memo says how VPN servers and Diameter servers use that shared secret.

questions: how does ikev2 use diameter with shared keys
ikev2 aaa authentication with shared keys

how is the ikev2 shared key derived
subtitle: How an IKEv2 server asks a Diameter server for the shared key it needs to authenticate a peer.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 can authenticate a peer with a shared key (SK), but the earlier Diameter work for Mobile IPv6 home agents only covered EAP-based authentication, so an IKEv2 server had no standard way to fetch an SK from the operator's Diameter server.
tldr.mechanism: A new Diameter application, IKESK (application identifier 11), has the IKEv2 server send an IKEv2-SK-Request carrying the peer's identity and the two IKEv2 nonces. The home AAA server derives the SK and returns it in a Key AVP in the IKEv2-SK-Answer.
tldr.outcome: IKEv2 servers can authorize and authenticate peers that use shared keys through the operator's Diameter infrastructure, with a default key derivation based on the nonces and the initiator identity. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 6738 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It complements RFC 5778 by covering shared-key authentication, and it relies on the Diameter base protocol in RFC 6733.

sections.title: The Problem and the Architecture
sections.content:
The Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2 (IKEv2) mutually authenticates two parties and sets up a Security Association (SA) that protects traffic with ESP or AH. IKEv2 allows several ways to authenticate a peer, including EAP, certificates and a Shared Key (SK). RFC 5778 already specified how a Mobile IPv6 home agent talks to a Diameter server when EAP or the Mobile IPv6 Authentication Protocol is used. It did not cover SK.

This document fills that gap. The IKEv2 peer talks IKEv2 to an IKEv2 server, and that server acts as a Diameter client toward the Home AAA (HAAA) Diameter server. The RFC's example is Mobile IPv6: the mobile node is the IKEv2 peer, the home agent is the IKEv2 server, and the home agent obtains the SK through the Diameter application defined here.

The RFC assumes the SK given to the peer and the SK delivered to the IKEv2 server are established or derived under the same rules, agreed by the external protocol on the peer side and the Diameter server side.
sections.plainLanguage: A visitor shows up at a gate with a secret code. The gate guard does not know the code, so the guard phones head office, which looks it up and tells the guard.

sections.title: How the Request and Answer Flow
sections.content:
When the IKEv2 server receives the IKE_AUTH message, it uses the identity in IDi, and the SPI if available, to find the right SK. If it has none, it MUST send an Authorize-Only IKEv2-SK-Request to the HAAA. The server fills User-Name from IDi when that is a meaningful identity such as a Network Access Identifier. It SHALL also include the IKEv2-Nonces AVP, with the initiator and responder nonces (Ni and Nr) from the initial exchange, and an IKEv2-Identity AVP holding IDi and, if the peer sent one, IDr.

The HAAA finds the keying material using User-Name and the initiator identity, derives the SK, and returns it in a Key AVP defined in RFC 6734. The Key-Type is set to IKEv2 SK (3), the Keying-Material AVP holds the SK, and a Key-Lifetime may be included. The receiver SHALL NOT use a key whose lifetime has expired. Once the IKEv2 server has the SK, it verifies AUTH in the IKE_AUTH message and, if that succeeds, sends the IKE message back to the peer.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard tells head office who the visitor says they are and two random numbers from the greeting. Head office works out the secret and sends it back, and the guard checks the visitor's code against it.

sections.title: Commands and AVPs
sections.content:
The new application is Diameter IKE SK (IKESK) with application identifier 11. It defines one command code, 329: IKEv2-SK-Request (IKESKR, with the 'R' bit set) and IKEv2-SK-Answer (IKESKA, 'R' bit cleared). The request MUST include IKEv2-Nonces and IKEv2-Identity, and MAY contain a Key-SPI AVP, which the HAAA then uses in addition to other parameters to identify the right SK. If the answer is successful it SHALL include the Key AVP.

The new AVPs are:

  • IKEv2-Nonces (587), grouped, containing Ni (588) and Nr (589), both OctetString.
  • IKEv2-Identity (590), grouped, containing Initiator-Identity (591) and optionally Responder-Identity (594).
  • Inside each identity AVP: ID-Type (592, Enumerated) and Identification-Data (593, OctetString), copied from the IDi or IDr payload.
sections.plainLanguage: The request is a form with the visitor's name and the two random numbers. The answer is a form with the secret, and perhaps an expiry date for it.

sections.title: Default Shared-Key Derivation
sections.content:
The selection of how the SK is derived is made by the external protocol between the peer and the Diameter server. When no other procedure is specified, this RFC gives a default that follows the method in Section 3.1 of RFC 5295: SK = KDF(PSK, key label | "\0" | Ni | Nr | IDi | length).

  • The KDF is the default one based on HMAC-SHA-256 from RFC 5295.
  • The PSK is whatever key the protocol using this application has, such as a long-term shared secret or an Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) from earlier EAP authentication.
  • The key label is sk4ikev2@ietf.org.
  • Length is a 2-octet unsigned integer, in network byte order, of the output key length in octets.

Applications that define their own derivation are strongly RECOMMENDED to use Ni and Nr, and RECOMMENDED to use IDi. IDr SHOULD NOT be used, because the IDr the peer asserts may differ from the IDr the IKEv2 responder returns, which would produce different SKs.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides mix the same ingredients in the same recipe: the master secret, the visitor's name and the two random numbers. If both follow the recipe, they end up with the same secret key.

sections.title: Session Management
sections.content:
The HAAA may keep Diameter session state or be stateless, which it indicates by including or leaving out the Auth-Session-State AVP in the answer. The IKEv2 server MUST support the Authorization Session State Machine from RFC 6733.

If the HAAA keeps state, the IKEv2 server SHALL send a Session-Termination-Request when it terminates the SA, and the HAAA acknowledges with a Session-Termination-Answer. The HAAA can also send an Abort-Session-Request to end the authorized session. When the IKEv2 server receives it, it MUST delete the corresponding IKE_SA and all CHILD_SAs set up through it.
sections.plainLanguage: If head office keeps a visitor log, the guard tells it when a visitor leaves. Head office can also order the guard to send a visitor out and close all their passes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of the Diameter base protocol apply, and the IKEv2 server and the Diameter server are assumed to be in a trusted relationship with appropriate protection between them, for example a shared secure network or transport-layer security. If Diameter agents or AAA brokers are in the path, the communication is only protected hop by hop, and any agent that processes an IKEv2-SK-Answer can see the contents of the Key AVP.

To avoid exposing a long-lived PSK, the HAAA derives the SK and returns only that. The RFC recommends short-lived secrets for derivation where available, and strongly recommends using the nonces in the request for key freshness and to limit the key's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Head office only hands out a one-time code, not the master secret. But anyone who listens on the phone line between them could hear the code, so the line must be kept private.
